The version of the prosecution is that vide application form/ bio data form dated 01.04.1992 the petitioner/ accused had applied for the post of Ancillary Worker in the Food Corporation of India,
Regional Office, New Delhi and he had wrongly mentioned his date of birth as 10.05.1968 in the said form as well as in the declaration form which was subsequently submitted.

The complainant, who is stated to be acquainted with the petitioner/ accused, filed a complaint dated 13.08.2015 with the police in this regard bringing these facts to the notice of the police and further informing that the correct date of birth of the petitioner/ accused is 01.08.1959.
Accordingly, on the complaint of the complainant the present FIR was registered.
3. During investigation, it was revealed that as per the school record of the the petitioner/ accused his correct date of birth is 01.08.1959.
The requisite information and documents were also collected from the Food Corporation of India.

The Food Corporation of India informed that the appointment of the petitioner/ accused was made to the post of Ancillary Worker on the basis of the application form/ bio Kishan Kumar v. State data form submitted by him, which was also attested by the labour union representative, as this was the prevalent practice at point of time and he had subsequently submitted a declaration form as well.

As per the said forms the date of birth of the petitioner/
accused was 10.05.1968.
The FCI further informed that there was no minimum or maximum age limit for the said employment and since there was no supporting document for the date of birth the same could not be verified.
4. After completion of investigation, charge-sheet was filed against the petitioner/ accused for the offences punishable under sections 420/468 of the IPC.

After consideration of the material available on record, vide order dated 13.05.2024 charge was ordered to be framed against the petitioner/
accused for the offence punishable under section 420 of the IPC.

The Ld. Trial Court, however, held that the petitioner/ accused had not submitted any supporting documents and had only wrongly mentioned his date of birth in the bio data form and the declaration form and therefore it cannot be said that he had forged any document and accordingly, the petitioner/ accused was discharged for the offence punishable under section 468 IPC.

Thereafter charge was framed against the petitioner/
accused for the offence punishable under section 420 IPC on 14.08.2024.
The petitioner/ accused has assailed the said orders in the present revision petition.
5. Ld.

Counsel for the petitioner has contended that the present complaint has been lodged by the respondent no. 2, who is an acquaintance, only to satisfy his personal grudge against the petitioner/
Kishan Kumar v. State accused.

It has further been contended that a departmental inquiry was conducted by the Food Corporation of India against the petitioner/ accused and the date of birth of the petitioner/ accused was corrected in the official records and the petitioner was retired on 31.07.2019.
It has further been contended that the ingredients of the offence under section 420 of the IPC are not made out against the petitioner/ accused.
It has further been contended that criminal prosecution cannot be used as an instrument of harassment.

accused

8. The scope of interference in revision proceedings is extremely limited and the same has been enunciated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court and the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in a number of judgments.

In the judgment titled as Sanjaysinh Ramrao Chavan v. Dattatray Galabrao Phalke as reported in (2015) 3 SCC123, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed:
"....14....Unless the order passed by the Magistrate is perverse or the view taken by the court is wholly unreasonable or there is non-consideration of any relevant material or there is palpable misreading of records

sentences.text: , the Revisional Court is not justified in setting aside the order, merely because another view is possible.
The Revisional Court is not meant to act as an appellate court.
The whole purpose of the revisional jurisdiction is to preserve the power in the court to do justice in accordance with the principles of criminal jurisprudence.
The revisional power of the court under Sections 397 to 401 CrPC is not to be equated with that of an appeal.

Unless the finding of the court, whose decision is sought to be revised, is shown to be perverse or untenable in law or is grossly erroneous or glaringly unreasonable or where the decision is based on no material or where the material facts are wholly ignored or where the judicial discretion is exercised arbitrarily or Kishan Kumar v. State capriciously, the courts may not interfere with decision in exercise of their revisional jurisdiction....."

9. In the judgment titled as Amit Kapoor v. Ramesh Chander reported as (2012) 9 SCC 460, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed:
"..........8.

sentences.text: Before examining the merits of the present case, we must advert to the discussion as to the ambit and scope of the power which the courts including the High Court can exercise under Section 397 and Section 482 of the Code.

Section 397 of the Code vests the court with the power to call for and examine the records of an inferior court for the purposes of satisfying itself as to the legality and regularity of any proceedings or order made in a case.
The object of this provision is to set right a patent defect or an error of jurisdiction or law.

There has to be a well- founded error and it may not be appropriate for the court to scrutinize the orders, which upon the Kishan Kumar vs State Of Nct Delhi And Ors on 8 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/97054354/
3 face of it bears a token of careful consideration and appear to be in accordance with law.

sentences.text: If one looks into the various judgments of this Court, it emerges that the revisional jurisdiction can be invoked where the decisions under challenge are grossly erroneous, there is no compliance with the provisions of law, the finding recorded is based on no evidence, material evidence is ignored or judicial discretion is exercised arbitrarily or perversely.
These are not exhaustive classes, but are merely indicative.
Each case would have to be determined on its own merits.

Another well-accepted norm is that the revisional jurisdiction of the higher court is a very limited one and cannot be exercised in a routine manner.
One of the inbuilt restrictions is that it should not be against an interim or interlocutory order.
The Court has to keep in mind that the exercise of revisional jurisdiction itself should not lead to injustice ex facie.

Where the Court is dealing with the question as to whether the charge has been framed properly and in accordance with law in a given case, it may be reluctant to interfere in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction unless the case substantially falls within the categories aforestated......"

10. In the judgment titled as Chandra Babu v. State, reported as (2015) 8 SCC 774, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed:

sentences.text: The scope of interference in a revision petition is extremely narrow.

It is well settled that Section 397 CrPC gives the High Courts or the Sessions Courts jurisdiction to consider the correctness, legality or propriety of any finding inter se an order and as to the regularity of the proceedings of any inferior court.

It is also well settled that while considering the legality, propriety or correctness of a finding or a conclusion, normally the revising court does not dwell at length upon the facts and evidence of the case.

A court in revision considers the material only to satisfy itself about the legality and propriety of the findings, sentence and order and refrains from substituting its own conclusion on an elaborate consideration of evidence......."

sentences.text:
On consideration of the authorities about the scope of Sections 227 and 228 of the Code, the following principles emerge:
(i) The Judge while considering the question of framing the charges under Section 227 CrPC has the undoubted power to sift and weigh the evidence for the limited purpose of finding out whether or not a prima facie case against the accused has been made out.
The test to determine prima facie case would depend upon the facts of each case.

(ii) Where the materials placed before the court disclose grave suspicion against the accused which has not been properly explained, the court will be fully justified in framing a charge and proceeding with the trial.

(iii) The court cannot act merely as a post office or a mouthpiece of the prosecution but has to consider the broad probabilities of the case, the total effect of the evidence and the documents produced before the court, any basic infirmities, etc.
However, at this stage, there cannot be a roving enquiry into the pros and cons of the Kishan Kumar v. State matter and weigh the evidence as if he was conducting a trial.

(iv) If on the basis of the material on record, the court could form an opinion that the accused might have committed offence, it can frame the charge, though for conviction the conclusion is required to be proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused has committed the offence.
(v) At the time of framing of the charges, the probative value of the material on record cannot be gone into but before framing a charge the court must apply its judicial mind on the material placed on record and must be satisfied that the Kishan Kumar vs State Of Nct Delhi And Ors on 8 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/97054354/
5 commission of offence by the accused was possible.
(vi) At the stage of Sections 227 and 228, the court is required to evaluate the material and documents on record with a view to find out if the facts emerging therefrom taken at their face value disclose the existence of all the ingredients constituting the alleged offence.
For this limited purpose, sift the evidence as it cannot be expected even at that initial stage to accept all that the prosecution states as gospel truth even if it is opposed to common sense or the broad probabilities of the case.
(vii) If two views are possible and one of them gives rise to suspicion only, as distinguished from grave suspicion, the trial Judge will be empowered to discharge the accused and at this stage, he is not to see whether the trial will end in conviction or acquittal....."
14.

sentences.text: Adverting to the facts of the present case, the application form/ bio-data form, on the basis of which the petitioner/ accused was selected for employment by the Food Corporation of India (FCI)

as well Kishan Kumar v. State as the declaration form which was subsequetly submitted by him, are available on record, and the date of birth of the petitioner/ accused reflected in the said forms is 10.05.1968.
However, the school records of the petitioner/ accused, which have been duly obtained by the investigating agency, reflect his date of birth as 01.08.1959.
It is reasonable to presume that the petitioner/ accused was aware of the contents of all of the aforesaid documents.
The discrepancy between the two dates of birth is significant and, prima facie, does not appear to be a result of any bona fide error.

15. By virtue of this fraudulent misrepresentation, the petitioner/ accused stood to gain an extension of approximately nine years in service, which would have resulted in the petitioner/ accused drawing salary and enjoying service-related benefits during this extended period as well.

While it is true that the FCI has submitted that there was no prescribed minimum or maximum age limit for the post in question, the conduct of the petitioner/ accused suggests a deliberate intention to secure a prolonged service tenure, thereby inducing FCI to disburse salary and benefits (which definitely constitute 'property' within the contemplation of section 420 IPC) for the extended duration as well.

16. Thus, prima facie, the manipulation of the date of birth appears to be attributable to the petitioner/ accused, and the surrounding circumstances give rise to a reasonable inference of dishonest intention on his part right from the very beginning.

Accordingly, a grave suspicion emerges that the petitioner/ accused dishonestly made a false Kishan Kumar v. State representation to FCI with respect to his date of birth, resulting in his appointment with a projected date of superannuation as 31.05.2028 which would have resulted in the petitioner/ accused drawing salary until that date.

sentences.text: In view of the foregoing, the essential ingredients constituting the offence under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) are prima facie made out.

17. It would be pertinent to refer to the judgment titled as Abhayanand Mishra v. State of Bihar reported as AIR 1961 SC 1698 wherein the accused had taken permission to appear for examination Kishan Kumar vs State Of Nct Delhi And Ors on 8 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/97054354/

Thus the salary and benefits which would have been disbursed to the petitioner/
accused during the extended period of service would definitely constitute property within the contemplation of section 420 IPC.
18.
On the other hand the judgments relied upon by the Ld. Counsel for the petitioner/ accused are not aplicable to the facts and circumstances of the case.
In Sushil Sethi v. State of Arunachal Pradesh the dispute related to supply of inferior quality materials under a contract by a company and the appellants were the MD and Director of the company.

State party and there are no specific allegations against the Managing Director or even the Director; and further there are no allegations to constitute vicarious liability.

Further in Inder Mohan Goswami v.
State of Uttaranchal the dispute related to an agreement to sell and it was held that the dispute was of civil nature and civil suit was also pending.

sentences.text: Thus the facts of the said cases were entirely different.

19. Another contention raised by the learned counsel for the petitioner/ accused is that the FSL report does not express any conclusive opinion regarding the purported signatures of the petitioner/
accused on the bio data form and declaration form.
However, the records of the Food Corporation of India (FCI) clearly indicate that the petitioner/ accused was granted employment on the basis of the said bio data form and declaration form.
Accordingly, it must be presumed that the date of birth mentioned therein was either filled in by the petitioner/ accused himself or was entered under his explicit instructions.
In any event, the petitioner/ accused is deemed to have full knowledge of the particulars furnished in his employment records with the FCI, including the date of birth mentioned therein.
He is equally presumed to be aware of the date of birth recorded in his school records.

Thus,
mere absence of a definitive FSL opinion on the signatures does not, at this stage, displace the presumption of his knowledge and involvement in the submission of the bio data form/ declaration form containing his incorrect date of birth.

20. The learned counsel for the petitioner/accused has further submitted that the petitioner/
accused retired on 31.07.2019 in Kishan Kumar v. State accordance with his correct date of birth,
and therefore, no actual financial loss was caused to the Food Corporation of India (FCI).

However,
this aspect is a matter to be considered and established during the course of trial.

In the event that,
upon conclusion of the trial, the learned Trial Court arrives at the finding that the petitioner/
accused merely attempted to deceive FCI without causing actual loss, he may still be convicted for the offence punishable under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, read with Section 511 IPC, by virtue of the provisions contained in Section 222 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
21. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case there does not appear to be any illegality or infirmity in the impugned orders of the Ld. Trial Court.
A prima facie case for the offence punishable u/s 420 of the IPC is made out against the petitioner/ accused for which charge has been rightly framed against him.

Considering the aforesaid facts and circumstances and bearing in mind the legal position discussed herein-above, I am of the opinion that no ground is made out for interfering with the impugned order on charge dated 13.05.2024 passed by Ld. JMFC-03, West District, Tis Hazari Courts, Delhi and the consequential order dated 14.05.2024 whereby charge was framed against the petitioner/ accused for the offence punishable under section 420 IPC.
The revision petition is therefore dismissed.
No costs.
